title: Astrophil and Stella 1
short: The opening sonnet of Sidney's sequence (written c. 1581-82, printed 1591), introducing Astrophil's search for words to win Stella.
body: Astrophil and Stella, 108 sonnets and eleven songs, was written in the early 1580s and circulated in manuscript; it was printed after Sidney's death in two unauthorised quartos of 1591 and in the 1598 folio of his works. Astrophil ('star-lover', Greek aster + philos) loves Stella ('star', Latin), widely identified with Penelope Devereux, who married Lord Rich in 1581. The archive's text keeps early printed spelling ('trueth', 'inuentions'). This first sonnet is a programmatic poem about how to write love poetry: it moves from a chain of hopes through failed imitation to the Muse's command to look within. Ringler's edition remains the standard text and commentary.

title: Form: alexandrine sonnet
short: Written in twelve-syllable hexameter lines (alexandrines), unusual in the sequence, rhyming ababababcdcdee.
body: Unlike most sonnets in the sequence, this one is in iambic hexameters (alexandrines), lines of six stresses and twelve syllables, which give it a long, deliberate movement suited to the rhetorical chain of lines 1-4. The octave uses only two rhymes in alternation (abababab), followed by cdcd and a closing couplet ee, a hybrid of Italian and English patterns. The long lines also make metre itself a subject: the poem goes on to complain of 'others feete' and of words that come 'halting'.

title: fayne (fain)
short: 'Fain' means eager or glad: loving sincerely and wishing to show it in verse. A pun on 'feign' is often heard.
body: 'Fain' (OED, fain, adj. and adv.) means gladly, willingly, eager. Many readers hear a pun on 'feign', to pretend or invent, which sets the sincerity of 'Louing in trueth' against the artifice of verse. The pun anticipates the sonnet's tension between truth and fiction, and Sidney's argument in the Defence that the poet 'nothing affirmeth, and therefore never lieth'. The spelling 'fayne' in the archive's text could represent either word.

title: the deere Shee
short: Stella, not yet named: 'Shee' as a noun, the beloved whose 'pleasure' in reading his pain is the poem's goal.
body: Using 'Shee' as a noun ('the dear she') was an Elizabethan idiom for 'the beloved woman'. The paradox 'pleasure of my paine' is typically Petrarchan: the lover's suffering, made into art, is offered as the lady's entertainment. Stella is not named until later in the sequence; the opening keeps her at a distance, as the object of a rhetorical campaign.

title: Pleasure ... grace: the gradatio
short: A rhetorical 'ladder' (climax or gradatio) in which each clause's last term begins the next: pleasure, reading, knowledge, pity, grace.
body: Lines 2-4 use the figure the Greeks called climax and the Latins gradatio, in which the final word of one clause becomes the first of the next: pleasure leads to reading, reading to knowing, knowledge to pity, pity to grace. Puttenham's Arte of English Poesie (1589) calls it 'the Marching figure' or 'the clyming figure', since 'Clymax' means a ladder. Sidney uses it to display the lover's calculated hopes as a chain of causes, a piece of reasoning that the rest of the poem shows to be ineffective. 'Grace' means the lady's favour, with an overtone of divine grace.

title: pittie ... grace
short: Pity is the lady's compassion; grace her favour, the reward the lover seeks, with religious overtones.
body: In the vocabulary of courtly love, the lady's 'pity' (mercy, compassion) is what the suffering lover hopes to arouse, and her 'grace' is the favour she grants. Both terms are also theological, and Sidney's sequence repeatedly plays on the overlap between devotion to Stella and religious devotion. The progression ends at the highest good the lover can hope for, which makes the collapse of his efforts in the following lines more marked.

title: to paint the blackest face of woe
short: Poetry as painting: he looked for apt words to depict his grief in its darkest colours.
body: 'Fit wordes' recalls the rhetorical principle of decorum, the suiting of style to matter. 'Paint' draws on the Renaissance commonplace, from Horace's ut pictura poesis, that poetry is a speaking picture; Sidney's Defence defines poetry as 'a speaking picture'. To paint the 'blackest face' of woe is to represent sorrow in its darkest, most moving form, so as to win pity. The verb also hints at cosmetic artifice, which the sonnet will reject.

title: inuentions
short: Invention (Latin inventio) is the rhetorical 'finding' of matter and arguments; he studies others' clever inventions.
body: In classical and Renaissance rhetoric, inventio, the first of the five parts of rhetoric, is the discovery of material and arguments (Latin invenire, to find). Here Astrophil studies other writers' ingenious inventions to 'entertain' Stella's wits, that is, imitation of models. At line 10 'Inuention' is personified as Nature's child, contrasting true invention arising from nature with borrowed, studied matter. The word 'fine' suggests elegance with a hint of over-refinement.

title: turning others leaues
short: Leafing through other poets' books, hoping their pages, like leaves, would shed fertile rain on his parched brain.
body: 'Leaves' are pages, and the image suggests a poet thumbing Petrarch and his imitators for material. The botanical sense of 'leaves' then generates the next lines' image of a 'fresh and fruitfull showre' falling on a 'Sunne-burnt braine': books are imagined as trees or clouds that might water a dry mind. The conceit mocks derivative love poetry, a target Sidney also attacks in the Defence.

title: Sunne-burnt braine
short: A brain scorched dry, needing a fertilising shower; perhaps also burned by Stella, the star or sun of the sequence.
body: The image of a parched brain longing for rain extends the metaphor of fertility; the heat might be that of love, or of the scorching influence of other writers. Since Stella is a star and later sonnets compare her to the sun, some readers see a hint that the beloved herself has dried his invention. In humoral physiology dryness was associated with melancholy and choler, and melancholy was the lover's disease.

title: halting
short: Limping: his words come out lamely, a metrical pun on verse 'feet'.
body: To 'halt' (OED, halt, v.1) is to limp; the word looks forward to 'others feete' in line 11, so that verse with faltering metre becomes a lame walker. The pun on metrical feet and walking was common in Renaissance discussions of verse. 'Wanting inuentions stay' means lacking the support (stay, a prop or brace) that invention would give, so the words cannot stand or walk properly.

title: Inuention Natures childe, fledde Stepdames studies blowes
short: Invention, Nature's child, flees the blows of Study, its stepmother: true creativity comes from nature, not laborious study.
body: Sidney allegorises a debate central to Renaissance poetics, between nature (natural talent, ingenium) and art (learning, study, imitation). Invention is Nature's offspring; Study is a stepmother, proverbially cruel, whose beatings drive the child away. The line does not wholly reject learning (Sidney was a deeply learned poet) but argues that study without native invention produces lifeless verse. It anticipates the Muse's advice to look inward, while also being itself a highly studied figure.

title: others feete
short: Other poets' metrical feet, and their footsteps: imitating them only trips him up like strangers on his road.
body: The phrase puns on metrical feet and on footsteps, so that other poets' verses, followed as models, become strangers who block his way. It continues the walking image from 'halting' and connects to the debate over imitation: following another writer's steps produces lines that do not belong to the poet. Ringler and Duncan-Jones gloss the pun in their notes. The image also anticipates Astrophil's later scorn, in sonnets 3, 6 and 15, for poets who borrow Petrarch's or Pindar's manner rather than finding their own.

title: great with Childe ... my throwes
short: The poet as a pregnant woman unable to give birth: full of things to say but helpless in labour pains (throes).
body: The childbirth metaphor for poetic creation is ancient (Plato's Symposium speaks of those pregnant in soul), and Sidney extends the family imagery of line 10. 'Throwes' are throes, the pangs of labour. The image is striking for a male poet and makes poetic composition a bodily ordeal. It sets up the final line, in which the Muse acts as a kind of midwife by telling him where the child is to be found.

title: Byting my tongue and penne
short: A gesture of the frustrated writer, recalling classical satire's image of the poet who bites his nails over his verses.
body: The gesture of self-punishment echoes a classical picture of the struggling writer. Persius (Satire 1.106) mocks bad verse that has never made its author pound his desk or taste his bitten nails, and Gildersleeve's commentary compares Horace (Satires 1.10.70), where the true poet scratches his head and gnaws his nails to the quick. Sidney's version turns the gesture into comedy: the poet bites his pen and his tongue, and beats himself 'for spite', that is, in vexation.

anchor: looke in thy heart and write
title: looke in thy heart and write
short: The Muse's famous command: write from what is within. Critics debate whether this means sincerity, or that Stella's image is written in his heart.
body: The Muse's rebuke ('Foole') and her instruction reverse the poem's laborious search: the matter lies within the poet. It is often read as a manifesto of sincerity and connects with the Defence, where Sidney complains that love poets 'coldly ... apply fiery speeches' and lack the 'forcibleness, or energia' of true feeling. But the line has been read more subtly: in Petrarchan convention the beloved's image is engraved in the lover's heart, so to look in his heart is to look at Stella, the true source of invention. Since the line closes a highly artful sonnet, many critics also see irony in its apparent rejection of art. 'Heart' also included thought and understanding in Renaissance usage.

title: Foole saide My muse to mee
short: His Muse, the classical goddess of poetry, abruptly calls him a fool, a dramatic turn in the final line.
body: The Muses were the nine daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne who inspire the arts. Here the poet's Muse intervenes as a speaking character, interrupting his self-torment with a blunt 'Foole'. The sudden shift from narrative to dramatic speech in the last line gives the sonnet a comic volta in the closing couplet. The archive text's capitalised 'My' and lack of quotation marks reflect early printed punctuation; modern editions punctuate the Muse's words as direct speech.
